prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 rows toward higher y, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet, and the starting architecture scores 0.000. With the default recipe the budget buys only 32 PPO updates (131k steps ÷ 4,096 per update), and 4 epochs per update use up compute that could pay for more samples. I suspect the 0.000 comes mostly from too few updates, not from a weak network. The default gamma of 0.95 also discounts the +1 exact-build bonus heavily over episodes of up to 33 steps. So two candidates keep the starting network and change only the recipe: 2 epochs on 128 envs, or 1 epoch on 64 envs. Both use more, smaller updates, gamma 0.99 and lambda 0.95. Since both started from zero, either one scoring above zero would show that recipe matters. The third candidate tests a new idea under a similar recipe: score each placement separately for each layer, then combine the layers with logsumexp, so the network can learn the landing layer.

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on dev and 0 on training success in the last 10% of training. Those trials changed the epoch count, sample count, update count, gamma and the per-layer head, and none of it made a difference. When even easy 6-brick training designs never get built, more tuning probably won't help. The world may not be what we assume. Every network so far uses a translation-equivariant conv head that scores the action at (t,y,x) from features at cell (y,x). If the real action-to-cell mapping is transposed, flipped or shifted ("this world may not behave as described"), that head cannot learn the policy. This round tests that directly. Each candidate has a dense, position-specific action head that can learn any mapping: (A) a plain MLP, (B) the starting network plus a dense head added to its logits, and (C) a small transformer with both a per-cell head and a dense head.

### Round 3
All 6 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and also 0 in training (last 10%). That covers conv, per-layer, MLP and transformer networks and recipes with 1 or 2 epochs and gamma 0.95 or 0.99. Several of those networks should be able to represent a decent placement rule, so representation alone is an unlikely cause. Two causes remain. (1) The world's mapping from action index to cell may differ from the stated one, for example transposed, flipped or with types interleaved. The conv heads would then score the wrong actions, and the dense heads are too sample-hungry to compensate. (2) The policy may collapse early, for example to an early DONE, because random placements often score negative. This round is a 2x2 design over {hedged action-mapping head, base net} x {ent 0.005, ent 0.03}; r1c1 already covers base net with ent 0.005. Any nonzero seed is a strong signal to exploit in round 4.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored 0.000 on both seeds, and every one also had 0 training success. The failures cover a wide range: the starting conv net, recipes using 1, 2 or 4 epochs, high entropy, per-layer scoring, a flat MLP, a dense head that can learn any action mapping, a transformer, and heads hedged against a different action mapping. Nothing beats seed noise, so the results cannot rank any idea. Because flexible-mapping networks also failed, a wrong action mapping is an unlikely sole cause. Two causes have not been tested: unstable optimisation (shared actor-critic trunk, unnormalised inputs, lr 1e-3) and long-horizon credit (gamma 0.99). This last round spreads its three trials across those causes. One keeps the starting net and uses a myopic, low-lr recipe. One adds per-cell normalisation and a separate critic. One uses a dilated trunk with global context so that DONE can see the whole grid. Any nonzero two-seed score would be the new best.

## Trial it ended with
name: Dilated trunk with global broadcast
hypothesis: Replaces the 5x5-receptive-field trunk with residual 3x3 convs at dilations 1, 2 and 4, plus a pooled global vector added back to every cell, all with per-cell LayerNorm. Each placement score and the DONE decision can then use whole-grid context: what is still missing, and which supports exist elsewhere. Refuted if both seeds stay at 0, which would mean limited receptive field is not the bottleneck.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 2 says: "If the real action-to-cell mapping is transposed, flipped or shifted... that head cannot learn the policy." "Shifted" is the right kind of spatial misalignment, but it is only one of several guesses. It is also placed in the action mapping, not in the observed target channels. The text never says the target is rolled 4 rows along y with wrap-around. Round 3 drops "shifted" from its list, and Round 4 calls a wrong mapping "an unlikely sole cause".
